USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the 90-day negotiation window opened at the G20 Buenos Aires dinner, pressing China to deliver on its promised agricultural purchases and structural commitments while holding current tariffs at 10% (List 3). Do not escalate toward the threatened 25% hike on ~$250B of imports this quarter — that would hit US consumers, retailers, and markets precisely as growth is cooling — and do not concede early while China has yet to fully deliver on purchases. Keep the Huawei/Meng and Canadian-detainee matters quarantined from the trade track where possible, as US and Chinese officials are both attempting to do.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate, not existential. The US holds the initiative and asymmetric leverage — it has imposed Section 301 tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese imports while China's retaliation covers only ~$60B (timeline: 2018-09-24). Fundamentals remain solid: consumer sentiment is 98.3, industrial production is up, and CPI is contained (country_health). But real drags exist: soybean exports to China are down ~97%, prices fell ~$2/bushel, and the administration has had to authorize a second ~$9.6B farmer-aid package (web search, CNN Dec 17-18) — material domestic political pressure in the farm belt. Markets show stress (10Y yield falling to ~2.77, Baa spreads widening, oil collapse) indicating cooling growth. The Huawei arrest of Meng Wanzhou (Dec 1) and China's detention of two Canadians (Dec 10) risk poisoning the truce, yet Kudlow and Chinese officials publicly insist the case stays separate from trade talks (CNBC Dec 7; NYT Dec 6). Given solid fundamentals and US leverage, threat sits just above neutral at +0.3; the recommendation is to negotiate (action_score +0.1) — advance the deal within Lighthizer's hard 90-day deadline without new escalation or premature concession, since China's own renewed soybean orders signal enough momentum that discarding it by escalating would be self-defeating.

US fundamentals strong: sentiment 98.3, IP up, CPI contained (country_health)

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Preserve and work the 90-day negotiation window opened at the Buenos Aires G20 dinner rather than escalate. Keep the Huawei/Meng affair quarantined from the trade track as much as possible, signal resolve on the Meng case through diplomatic channels, but avoid further retaliatory escalation that could collapse the truce and trigger the scheduled January 1 rise of List 3 tariffs from 10% to 25%. The priority now is holding the talks to prevent the far costlier 25% outcome.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is high but short of existential (+0.45). Already-active US tariffs cover roughly $250B of Chinese exports (25% on the $50B List 1/2 plus 10% on the ~$200B List 3 effective Sept 24). The Dec 1 arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou at US request is direct firm-level targeting of a flagship tech company — the CHN +0.5 anchor — and Chinese firms in export hubs report squeezed margins, front-loaded orders, and yuan depreciation of ~9% over six months approaching the psychologically important 7 level, all on top of an economy already slowing to near-decade-low growth. These are genuine, material stresses. Yet the situation is not existential because the Jan 1 escalation to 25% is currently suspended (Dec 1) and both sides have an incentive to talk. On action, escalation would be self-defeating: Beijing cannot match the US dollar-for-dollar (US ~$506B imports vs China ~$130B), and provoking a collapse would bring down the 25% hike in weeks, hitting export hubs far harder. China has already retaliated with the Dec 10 detention of two Canadians to demonstrate resolve on Meng without touching the trade track. The right posture is hold-and-negotiate — maintain the truce, manage the Meng affair diplomatically, and avoid new escalation that risks the January cliff.
